title: Capstone Part 1: Discovery, Design, and Planning

content:
# Capstone Part 1: Discovery, Design, and Planning ##### The automation nobody wanted A consultant spent three weeks building an elegant automation for a manufacturing client: a real-time dashboard fed by six systems, with alerts, an AI summary, and a beautiful architecture. Technically excellent. Nobody used it. In the kickoff meeting, the operations head had mentioned in passing that the dashboard "would be nice to have someday." What actually consumed his team's time — eleven hours a week — was manually chasing suppliers for delivery confirmations. Nobody asked. The consultant heard "dashboard," got excited, and built the wrong thing beautifully. The most expensive mistakes in automation are made before any tool is opened. Your capstone starts here, with the unglamorous work that determines whether the next two days produce something valuable or something impressive and useless. Business process management research (van der Aalst et al., 2003) has said this for decades: understand and often *redesign* the process before you automate it. Automating a bad process just produces bad outcomes faster. ##### Identifying a high-value opportunity Pick your capstone process using evidence, not enthusiasm. Score candidates on five dimensions: | Criterion | Question | Good sign | |---|---|---| | **Frequency** | How often does it happen? | Daily or many times weekly | | **Duration** | How long does each instance take? | 5+ minutes of human time | | **Rule-based** | Are the decisions consistent? | Yes — if/then, not judgment calls | | **Digital inputs** | Is the data already in systems? | Yes — forms, emails, APIs, sheets | | **Error cost** | What happens when it goes wrong? | Real, measurable pain | The value calculation is simple arithmetic and you should do it explicitly: ```text Annual hours saved = (minutes per run × runs per month × 12) / 60 Annual value = hours saved × fully-loaded hourly cost + errors avoided × cost per error Example — supplier chasing: 22 min × 45 runs/month × 12 = 11,880 min = 198 hours/year 198 h × ₹600/h = ₹1,18,800 plus ~6 missed deliveries/year × ₹8,000 rework = ₹48,000 Total annual value ≈ ₹1,66,800 (build effort: ~20 hours) ``` Avoid these traps when choosing: processes that run twice a year (not worth it), processes requiring genuine human judgment (empathy, negotiation, legal sign-off), processes about to be replaced by a new system, and processes where the data lives only on paper. Good capstone candidates from real student projects: order-to-invoice pipelines, lead capture and routing, support ticket triage with AI classification, recruitment application processing, content publishing pipelines, and event registration with reminders. ##### Process mapping: as-is versus to-be **The as-is map** documents what happens *today*, honestly — including the workarounds, the "then I copy it into a second sheet because the first one is wrong," and the ninety-minute wait for approval. How to build one properly: watch someone do it (do not just ask), write each step with its actor, tool and duration, note every decision point and every handoff, and mark where errors and delays actually occur. Then have the person who does the work review it. They will correct you, and those corrections are the most valuable information in the project. ```text AS-IS: Supplier delivery confirmation (22 min per order, 45×/month) 1. Ops opens shared inbox 2 min 2. Finds PO confirmation emails, one per supplier 4 min 3. Opens the tracking sheet, finds matching PO row 3 min ← error-prone 4. Copies confirmed date, quantity, price 5 min ← manual re-keying 5. If mismatch vs PO → emails supplier, waits 4 min ← delay 6. Updates status column 2 min 7. Pastes summary into the WhatsApp group 2 min Pain: re-keying errors (~1 in 15), 3 systems, no audit trail, nothing happens if the ops person is on leave. ``` **The to-be map** is your design. Critically, it is not the as-is map with robots substituted for humans — **first eliminate and simplify, then automate.** Steps 3 and 6 above merge into a single database update; step 7 becomes an aggregated digest; the mismatch check becomes a rule. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Supplier confirmation email arrives] --> B[Verify sender + parse with AI
extract PO no, date, qty, price] B --> C{Parse confidence >= 0.8
and PO exists?} C -->|no| H[Human review queue
+ Slack notice] C -->|yes| D[(Update orders table
status, confirmed_date)] D --> E{Matches PO
within tolerance?} E -->|yes| F[Mark confirmed] E -->|no| G[Flag discrepancy
+ draft supplier email for approval] F --> I[Daily 6pm digest to WhatsApp/Slack] G --> I H --> I ``` Then state the delta plainly: **22 minutes → ~2 minutes of exception handling per day; re-keying errors eliminated; full audit trail; works when the ops person is on leave.** ##### Choosing tools and architecture Apply your Day 12 framework, and write down the reasoning — the assignment requires it. Work through the questions in order: Is the data regulated or subject to residency rules? Who maintains this in six months? Do the required integrations exist? What is the realistic volume × steps? Does the logic need arrays, loops or long-running state? Is there capability to run a server? How fast must it ship? Then record the decision in a table that shows you considered alternatives: ```text DECISION: n8n (self-hosted on a ₹700/month VPS) Considered: Zapier — rejected: 45 runs × 9 steps = 405 tasks/mo is fine, but no affordable AI + custom parsing, and client wants data on-prem Make.com — viable second choice: good iterators, cheap operations; rejected only because supplier emails contain PII the client wants kept in India n8n — CHOSEN: self-hosted (data residency), Code node for parsing, per-execution pricing, Postgres already available Supporting components: Postgres (Supabase) — order state, dedup, audit trail OpenAI gpt-4o-mini — email field extraction (~₹40/month at this volume) Slack — exceptions and daily digest ``` ##### Defining the data model and integrations Design the data before the workflow. This is the step that most distinguishes a planned project from an improvised one. ```sql -- Core state table for the capstone CREATE TABLE purchase_orders ( po_number TEXT PRIMARY KEY, supplier_email TEXT NOT NULL, expected_date DATE NOT NULL, expected_qty INT NOT NULL, expected_price NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL, confirmed_date DATE, confirmed_qty INT, confirmed_price NUMERIC(12,2), status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'awaiting_confirmation' CHECK (status IN ('awaiting_confirmation','confirmed', 'discrepancy','manual_review','cancelled')), updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now() ); CREATE TABLE processed_emails ( -- idempotency guard message_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, processed_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), po_number TEXT REFERENCES purchase_orders(po_number) ); ``` Alongside it, list every integration with the specifics you will need: system, direction, auth method, the exact operations used, rate limits, and what happens if it is unavailable. Doing this now surfaces blockers — "the supplier portal has no API" — while they are still cheap to solve. ##### Success metrics and risk assessment **Metrics must be defined before you build**, and each needs a baseline, a target, and a measurement method. Vague goals ("make it more efficient") cannot be evaluated, which conveniently means the project can never be judged a failure — and that is exactly why they are worthless. ```text METRIC BASELINE TARGET HOW MEASURED Processing time/order 22 min < 3 min run log durations Re-keying errors/month ~3 0 discrepancy audit Confirmation lag ~7 hours < 15 min received → recorded Ops hours/month 16.5 h < 2 h time log Automation success rate n/a > 97% runs table AI extraction accuracy n/a > 95% sample 50, review Cost/month n/a < ₹1,200 VPS + API spend ``` **Risks** need naming and mitigating, in a table you can show a client: | Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation | |---|---|---|---| | Supplier changes email format | High | Medium | AI extraction (layout-independent) + confidence threshold + human queue | | AI extracts a wrong value | Medium | High | Validate against PO; discrepancies never auto-approve | | Email provider outage | Low | Medium | Retry with backoff; nothing is lost, only delayed | | Duplicate processing | Medium | High | `processed_emails` primary key; idempotent updates | | Key person leaves (you) | Medium | High | Full README, exported workflow in Git, handover session | | Scope creep | High | Medium | Written scope; changes go to a phase 2 list | | PII in supplier emails | Certain | Medium | Self-hosted, redacted logs, 90-day retention | Note that the mitigations are *design decisions*, not intentions. "Be careful" is not a mitigation; "discrepancies never auto-approve" is. ##### Common pitfalls - **Building before understanding** — the dashboard story. - **Automating the as-is process** without simplifying it first. - **Not talking to the people who do the work** — they know the exceptions. - **No baseline measurement** — you cannot prove improvement you never measured. - **Choosing the tool first** and bending the requirements to fit. - **Ignoring the exception path.** The 20% of weird cases is where 80% of the work lives. - **Over-scoping the capstone.** One process, done fully and well, beats three done partially. - **No written scope** — the door through which scope creep walks. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task is your **project brief**, one to two pages: the problem and its quantified cost, an **as-is process map**, a **to-be design diagram**, **chosen tools with justification**, the **data model**, **success metrics**, and **key risks**. Write it for a client, not for a grader — that framing forces clarity. The mini project is the full **Part 1 planning package**, formally documented: both process maps, architecture and tool decisions with rationale, the integration and data-model plan, defined metrics, and the risk-and-mitigation table. Commit it to your capstone repository as `docs/01-plan.md`. Then, before you build anything tomorrow, **show it to someone who knows the process** and ask what you got wrong. They will tell you, and that conversation is worth more than a day of coding. For the assignment, **justify your tool and architecture choices in writing**, referencing cost, complexity, data privacy and volume, and explain **how you will measure success**. Include the alternatives you rejected and why — a decision with visible reasoning is what senior engineers produce, and it is precisely what interviewers probe for. ##### Key takeaways - Choose the process with evidence: frequency × duration × error cost, with digital inputs and rule-based decisions. - Map the as-is honestly by watching the work, then design a to-be that eliminates and simplifies before automating. - Justify tool choices against cost, maintainer, integrations, volume, logic complexity and data residency — and record the alternatives you rejected. - Design the data model and list every integration before building; this surfaces blockers while they are still cheap. - Define baselines, targets and measurement methods up front, and turn each identified risk into a concrete design decision.
